title: Βάτραχος ⟨ἰατρός⟩ καὶ ἀλώπηξ
titleEn: The Frog Physician and the Fox
part: The Frog Physician and the Fox (Chambry 69 · Perry 289)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 69 (= Perry 289). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄντος ποτὲ βατράχου ἐν τῇ λίμνῃ καὶ τοῖς ζῴοις πᾶσιν ἀναβοήσαντος· « Ἐγὼ ἰατρός εἰμι φαρμάκων ἐπιστήμων, » ἀλώπηξ ἀκούσασα ἔφη· « Πῶς σὺ ἄλλους σώσεις, σαυτὸν χωλὸν ὄντα μὴ θεραπεύων ; »
sentences.tr: Ontos pote batrachou en tēi limnēi kai tois zōiois pasin anaboēsantos· « Egō iatros eimi pharmakōn epistēmōn, » alōpēx akousasa ephē· « Pōs sy allous sōseis, sauton chōlon onta mē therapeuōn ; »
sentences.l: A frog being once in the pond and having called out to all the animals: « I am a physician, knowing in drugs, » a fox, having heard, said: « How will you save others, not curing yourself, lame as you are? »
sentences.i: There was once a frog in the pond who called out to all the animals: « I am a physician, and I know my drugs »; and a fox who heard him said: « How will you save others, when you do not cure your own lameness? »
sentences.n: One genitive absolute with two participles (ὄντος … καὶ … ἀναβοήσαντος) carries the whole first half — Greek is content to leave the frog outside the main clause altogether. The Greek title reads Βάτραχος ⟨ἰατρός⟩ καὶ ἀλώπηξ; the angle brackets are Chambry's own supplement. ἐπιστήμων takes a genitive of what one is knowing in. μή rather than οὐ with the participle θεραπεύων marks it as conditional, 'if/when you do not cure'. The jab lands on the frog's own crooked gait, χωλόν.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι ὁ παιδείας ἀμύητος ὑπάρχων, πῶς ἄλλους παιδεῦσαι δυνήσεται ;
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti ho paideias amyētos hyparchōn, pōs allous paideusai dynēsetai ;
sentences.l: The fable shows that — he who is uninitiated in education, how will he be able to educate others?
sentences.n: The sentence abandons its own construction: it opens with ὅτι as though a statement were coming and ends as a question. That break is in the Greek and is left standing here. ἀμύητος is the word for one not admitted to the mysteries — schooling is imagined as a rite one is initiated into.
